newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges Medicare compromise, budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges Medicare compromise, budget deal.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday urged Congress to pass balanced-budget legislation and offered a way to bridge an impasse on the sensitive issue of charging wealthy citizens higher Medicare premiums.

Speaking after a meeting with his budget advisers, Clinton appeared to be trying to ensure that negotiations to enact the balanced-budget accord he reached in May with congressional Republicans do not come unravelled.
"I believe it's very important now to complete the job and get a balanced budget agreement," Clinton told reporters after the meeting in the White House Cabinet Room.

Clinton also endorsed a version of a controversial Senate plan to raise Medicare premiums on the wealthy, an issue that has stalled negotations to resolve differences in budget bills passed by the House and Senate.

Responding to Republican concerns the increase would been seen as a tax, Clinton suggested the money be collected by the Treasury Department -- which would earmark it for the Medicare Trust Fund -- rather than by the Internal Revenue Service.

"We think that would ease a lot of the Republican, and frankly some of the Democratic, concerns that we wouldn't look like a tax increase," Clinton said, adding, "I'm very hopeful (this) will break the impasse."

The House of Representatives and Senate have each passed spending and tax bills to balance the budget and negotiators for both houses of Congress, with input from the White House, have been seeking to hammer out compromise legislation.
Clinton's Medicare proposal got a cautious reaction from Congress, with some Republicans calling it a positive step but still problematic.

"I don't think he's got it yet, but I view that as a positive move," Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, told reporters. "It is important to come up with some blended system that would not make this just a tax collection by the IRS ... We just can't have that."

"It may be a movement in the right direction," said Representative Bill Archer, the Texas Republican who chairs the House Ways and Means Committee. But he added a note of scepticism, saying, "The only collection arm I know at Treasury is IRS."

Sen. Pete Domenici, the New Mexico Republican who chairs the Senate Finance Committee, said he would look at the idea but added, "If it has something in there that really has IRS in it but you're covering it up, it may never sell."

As described by White House spokesman Mike McCurry, under Clinton's proposal the Treasury would send citizens a form to determine whether they should pay the higher premium. If so, they would write a check to the Medicare Trust Fund which would be due the same day as their income taxes, April 15.
Although McCurry initially said the check for the Treasury could be included with regular income tax returns, other White House officials said the details were not set.
McCurry acknowledged the arrangement seemed something of a fig leaf, quoting one senior White House official as saying, "It is a cosmetic solution to a cosmetic problem."
Clinton said he offered the change to salvage the proposal, which has been strongly opposed by House members who fear the move would create a political backlash against them.

Historically, the influential American Association of Retired Persons and other seniors groups have opposed any effort to raise Medicare premiums. In the 1980s, the lobby for the elderly forced Congress to reverse a similar plan.
Clinton, however, appeared to suggest the politics of the issue have changed and most U.S. citizens would back a rise.

"My best judgment is that a big majority of the American people will support this," he said, adding, "I would be happy to defend the vote of any member of Congress -- Democrat or Repulican -- who votes for this."
Florida Republican Sen. Connie Mack, whose state includes a large number of retirees, appeared to disagree, "He's given us permission to shoot ourselves in the foot on Medicare."
